newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS Web site gives surfers central bank access.
newsitem.headline: BIS Web site gives surfers central bank access.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) has set up a Web Site on the Internet that also gives surfers easy access to browse through the sites of several central banks.
The BIS home page, which went live only days ago, has been set up under the strictest possible security principles to shield confidential files from any hackers, BIS officials said.
The web site is the latest example of central banks and economic institutions using the Internet to reach a larger audience, in line with policies of increased transparency.
The primary purpose for creating the home page is to distribute more easily the growing number of working papers and reports published through the BIS, a central bank to the worlds' central banks.
Last year the BIS, which provides a secretariat for committees that discuss global banking supervision, payments systems and financial market structures, published some 3,000 pages.
In addition to committee reports, BIS also publishes data on banking and financial markets and an influential annual report.

The BIS site -- http://www.bis.org/ -- opens with a picture of the organisation's cooling-tower style headquarters and contains sections that display information about the BIS, its press releases, publications and central banks.

The publications' section gives an overview of publications from the various committees that make up the BIS, the world's oldest international financial institution, owned and controlled by central banks around the world.
The home pages of 12 national central banks are also linked to the BIS site.
They include the central banks and monetary authorities of Austria, Brazil, Canada, Estonia, Finland, Hong Kong, India, Mexico, New Zealand, Thailand, Britain and the United States.
Germany's Bundesbank is absent, but officials have said they are considering publishing on the Internet.
Central bank pages include key information about the central banks and their history, financial and economic data, regulatory issues, publications and news releases.
The U.S. Federal Reserve Board's home page is also linked with other district reserve banks, including the St. Louis federal reserve, one of the pioneers in setting up a home page.

"It is a more convenient and quicker way to distribute information than through the mail," said Charles Henderson of the St. Louis Fed, noting there are between 12,000 and 15,000 "hits" on the central bank's home page every week.

Among the more popular pages with economists and consultants is FRED -- Federal Reserve Economic Data -- which includes historical and financial data, such as daily interest rates, monetary and business indicators for the states covered by the St. Louis Fed.
In addition to professional uses, Henderson said the home pages also "helps people understand what the institution does. It demystifies the Federal Reserve."
Worries about hackers finding their way into sensitive central bank files influences the maintenance of the web site.
A stand-alone computer serves the home page to secure "fire walls" and only a limited number of people are permitted to load information onto the web site, Henderson said.
